newsitem.title: CHINA: China voices concern over Islamic fundamentalism.
newsitem.headline: China voices concern over Islamic fundamentalism.

text.p: Chinese leaders have expressed concern over the threat from Islamic fundamentalism, Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said on Wednesday.
Levy said the two nations had similar views on the issue.
"The issue came up in the talks (with Chinese leaders)," Levy told a news conference in Beijing on the last day of his three-day visit. "I think we have a very similar view on this."
He was speaking a day after reports that three bomb blasts in Urumqi, China's western, Moslem-majority city, had killed five people and injured as many as 60.

"Every attempt to turn religion into a weapon becomes extremely dangerous, it is something that knows no boundaries," Levy said. "It is like sand, it can be transported by the wind from one place to to another.
"I did not mean Islam in general, I am pointing at those who in the name of Islam are developing a sort of poison and danger and trying to threaten other people," he said.
During his visit, Levy met President Jiang Zemin, Premier Li Peng, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and Vice Premier Li Lanqing. He did not say which leader mentioned the issue.

Officials and residents in Urumqi said at least five people were killed and 60 people wounded by three blasts on Tuesday that shattered the calm prevailing in China since the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping a week ago.
The blasts came within five minutes of each other in separate parts of the city.
It was the first violence reported in restive Xinjiang since anti-Chinese riots in the region's town of Yining on February 5 and 6 left nine people dead and 198 wounded.
Chinese police arrested up to 300 people after that riot in Xinjiang, a region that Moslem separatists call East Turkestan.
The official said one of the bombs on Tuesday was on a bus in the city centre, and a second was on a bus that had passed by a radio station.
The bombs exploded around 6.40 p.m. (1040 GMT).
Officials said they suspected Moslem separatists were responsible.
Xinjiang, bordering Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly Moslem Central Asian states, was shaken last year by bombings and attacks on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
